title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Identify the primary structural function of a suspended work platform.
student: What is the primary structural function of the suspended platform system shown in the industry image?
instructor: The system supports workers, equipment, or other loads at an elevated position and transfers their weight through the suspension members to an overhead lifting or supporting system.

title: External Loading
learningObjectives: Identify the gravitational and eccentric loading acting on a suspended platform.
student: What external loads would normally act on a suspended work platform during use or lifting?
instructor: The platform carries downward gravitational loads from the platform itself and from workers, tools, equipment, or other payloads. If the supported load is located away from the center, the suspension system also experiences an eccentric loading condition that produces unequal suspension forces.

title: Supports and Restraints
learningObjectives: Describe how a suspended platform is supported and what force its suspension members transmit.
student: How is the platform supported, and what type of forces can the suspension members transmit?
instructor: The platform is supported from above through cables, slings, chains, or similar tensile members connected to an overhead lifting or support system. These members primarily transmit tensile force.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace the dominant load path through the physical suspended-platform system.
student: Trace the dominant load path from the supported load to the overhead lifting or supporting system.
instructor: The load is transferred from the payload into the platform, from the platform into the suspension members, and from the suspension members into the overhead lifting or supporting structure.

title: Effect of Eccentric Loading
learningObjectives: Predict how eccentric load position affects suspension forces and platform tilt.
student: What would you expect to happen if the supported load is positioned closer to one side of the platform rather than near its center?
instructor: The suspension members would generally carry unequal tensile forces. Members closer to the eccentric load tend to carry greater force, causing unequal elastic elongations and a corresponding tilt of the platform.

title: Relevant Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Identify the deformation responses governing platform position and orientation.
student: If the engineering concern is the position and orientation of the platform after loading, what mechanical responses must be considered?
instructor: The elastic elongation of the suspension members, the resulting vertical motion of the platform, and any rotation or tilt caused by differences in elongation between suspension points must be considered.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify loading, geometry, and material parameters controlling displacement and tilt.
student: What loading, geometric, and material characteristics would you expect to influence the displacement and tilt of the suspended system?
instructor: Relevant characteristics include the magnitude and location of the supported load, the length and cross-sectional size of the suspension members, the material stiffness of the suspension members, and the spacing between suspension points.
gradingNotes: At this stage, students should identify physical dependencies rather than instructor-model symbols or equations.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Create a mechanics model that preserves the dominant load path and deformation mechanisms.
student:
Convert the real suspended-platform system into a simplified Mechanics of Materials model that preserves the suspended platform, tensile suspension members, overhead supports, load location, suspension-point spacing, and the possibility of vertical displacement and rotation.

Student model / free-body diagram space
instructor: A suitable idealization uses rigid horizontal members supported by deformable axial tension members. Several equivalent student models are acceptable if they preserve the dominant load path and deformation mechanisms.
gradingNotes: Students should complete their own idealization before viewing the instructor reference model.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the equivalent suspended-system model.
student: State the assumptions used to convert the real suspended system into a simplified mechanics model.
instructor: Reasonable assumptions include static loading; rigid platform members; straight, vertical, linearly elastic suspension members; small deformation and small rotation; negligible suspension-member self-weight; idealized pinned/eye connections; and a rigid overhead support.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the equilibrium, deformation, and compatibility solution sequence.
student: Before calculating, describe the analysis sequence required to determine vertical displacement and tilt.
instructor: Use rigid-body equilibrium to determine suspension-member forces, calculate axial elongation of each deformable member, use rigid-body compatibility to obtain point displacements, and then determine platform translation and small-angle rotation from the displacement differences.

title: Boundary Conditions and Unknown Wire Forces
learningObjectives: Identify the boundary conditions and unknown forces in the instructor reference model.
student: From the instructor reference diagram, identify the boundary conditions and unknown wire forces.
instructor: The ceiling anchors at E and F are fixed. The four unknown wire forces are TED, TFC, TAH, and TBC, acting vertically along the wires. Members AB and DC are modeled as rigid bodies.

title: Equilibrium of Lower Rigid Member AB
learningObjectives: Determine lower-wire forces under eccentric loading.
student: Draw the free-body diagram of lower member AB and solve for the forces in the lower wires AH and BC.
instructor: For member AB: TAH + TBC = P. Taking moments about A gives TBCLAB = PxP. Therefore TBC = {{P}}({{x_P}})/{{L_AB}} = {{platform_T_BC_lb}} lb, and TAH = {{P}} - {{platform_T_BC_lb}} = {{platform_T_AH_lb}} lb.
gradingNotes: This step demonstrates how eccentric loading causes unequal lower-wire forces.

title: Equilibrium of Upper Rigid Member DC
learningObjectives: Determine upper-wire forces from equilibrium of the upper rigid member.
student: Draw the free-body diagram of upper member DC and solve for the forces in the upper wires ED and FC.
instructor: The lower wires apply downward forces of {{platform_T_AH_lb}} lb at H and {{platform_T_BC_lb}} lb at C. For member DC: TED + TFC = {{P}} lb. Taking moments about D gives TFCLDC = TAHxDH + TBCLDC. Thus TFC = [{{platform_T_AH_lb}}({{x_DH}}) + {{platform_T_BC_lb}}({{L_DC}})]/{{L_DC}} = {{platform_T_FC_lb}} lb and TED = {{platform_T_ED_lb}} lb.

title: Wire Elongations
learningObjectives: Calculate elongation of all four wires using consistent inch-pound units.
student: Calculate the elongation of each wire using δ = FL/(AE). Use consistent inch-pound units.
instructor: Using Lu = {{L_u}} ft = {{platform_L_u_in}} in, Ll = {{L_l}} ft = {{platform_L_l_in}} in, Aw = {{A_w}} in2, and Ew = {{E_w}} ksi = {{platform_E_w_psi}} psi: δAH = {{platform_delta_AH_in}} in, δBC = {{platform_delta_BC_in}} in, δED = {{platform_delta_ED_in}} in, and δFC = {{platform_delta_FC_in}} in.

title: Displacement of Point H on Upper Member DC
learningObjectives: Use rigid-body compatibility to determine displacement at an intermediate point.
student: Using rigid-body compatibility of upper member DC, determine the vertical displacement of point H.
instructor: The downward displacement of D equals δED = {{platform_delta_ED_in}} in and the downward displacement of C equals δFC = {{platform_delta_FC_in}} in. Since H is {{x_DH}}/{{L_DC}} of the way from D to C, δH = δD + (δC - δD)({{x_DH}}/{{L_DC}}) = {{platform_delta_H_in}} in downward.

title: Displacement of Endpoints A and B of Lower Member AB
learningObjectives: Combine upper support motion and lower-wire elongation to determine endpoint displacements.
student: Determine the downward displacement of points A and B on the lower rigid member.
instructor: Point A is attached below H through wire AH, so δA = δH + δAH = {{platform_delta_H_in}} + {{platform_delta_AH_in}} = {{platform_delta_A_in}} in downward. Point B is attached below C through wire BC, so δB = δC + δBC = {{platform_delta_FC_in}} + {{platform_delta_BC_in}} = {{platform_delta_B_in}} in downward.

title: Vertical Displacement of the Load
learningObjectives: Determine load-point displacement from the lower member's endpoint motions.
student: Determine the vertical displacement of the load point on lower member AB.
instructor: The load is xP/LAB = {{x_P}}/{{L_AB}} of the way from A to B. Therefore δP = δA + (δB - δA)({{x_P}}/{{L_AB}}) = {{platform_delta_load_in}} in downward.

title: Tilt Angle of Lower Member AB
learningObjectives: Calculate and interpret the small-angle tilt of lower member AB.
student: Determine the small-angle tilt of lower member AB after loading.
instructor: The tilt magnitude is |θAB| ≈ |δB - δA|/LAB = |{{platform_delta_B_in}} - {{platform_delta_A_in}}|/{{platform_L_AB_in}} = {{platform_theta_AB_rad}} rad = {{platform_theta_AB_deg}}°. The A end drops more than the B end, so AB tilts {{platform_lower_tilt_direction}}.

title: Tilt Angle of Upper Member DC
learningObjectives: Calculate and interpret the small-angle tilt of upper member DC.
student: Determine the small-angle tilt of upper member DC after loading.
instructor: The tilt magnitude is |θDC| ≈ |δC - δD|/LDC = |{{platform_delta_FC_in}} - {{platform_delta_ED_in}}|/{{platform_L_DC_in}} = {{platform_theta_DC_rad}} rad = {{platform_theta_DC_deg}}°. The D end drops more than the C end, so DC tilts {{platform_upper_tilt_direction}}.

title: Stiffness-Based Interpretation
learningObjectives: Identify the dominant deformation contribution and mechanics-based ways to reduce it.
student: Which deformation contribution most strongly affects the load displacement, and what change would reduce displacement or tilt?
instructor: The largest single elongation occurs in wire {{platform_dominant_wire}}, which carries {{platform_dominant_force_lb}} lb and has length {{platform_dominant_length_ft}} ft. Increasing suspension-member area, using a larger elastic modulus, shortening the deformable length, or reducing load eccentricity would reduce displacement and tilt.

title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Summarize the deformation response and recommend a mechanics-based improvement.
student: Based on the calculated displacement and tilt, summarize how the eccentric loading affects the suspended platform. Identify the suspension member that contributes most strongly to the deformation and recommend one mechanics-based change that would reduce platform displacement or tilt.
instructor: The eccentric load produces unequal suspension forces and therefore unequal elongations. The load point moves approximately {{platform_delta_load_in}} in downward. The lower rigid member tilts by approximately {{platform_theta_AB_rad}} rad, while the upper rigid member tilts by approximately {{platform_theta_DC_rad}} rad. Wire {{platform_governing_wire}} carries the largest force, and wire {{platform_dominant_wire}} has the largest elongation. Increasing suspension-member axial stiffness AE/L or reducing load eccentricity would reduce platform displacement and tilt.
gradingNotes: Strength, connector stress, fatigue, and buckling are outside the base problem because the required allowables and connector details are not part of the supplied data.
